main_point.en: Our lifestyle should point to Jesus and bring Him glory.

christ_connection.en: Jesus showed us how to decrease when He lowered Himself in obedience to the Father’s will and came to earth as a human. He took on our sin and paid our debt so that we could have right relationship with the Father and forgiveness for our sin. Jesus pointed all glory to the Father and took on the role of a servant.

content.en: 22 After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. 23 John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized 24 (for John had not yet been put in prison). 25 Now a discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification. 26 And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him.” 27 John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. 28 You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’ 29 The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. 30 He must increase, but I must decrease.”

31 “He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. 32 He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony. 33 Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true. 34 For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. 35 The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. 36 Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”
Leaders: Consider how you can point to Jesus instead of yourself. Even as leaders, we struggle with pointing to Jesus only. May we intentionally decrease and position Jesus above ourselves.

“The Baptizer is treated not merely as a historical person, but he is also employed as a character symbol who is to be contrasted directly with Jesus. He is witness; Jesus is the Light (1:7-8). He is voice; Jesus is the Word (1:14,23). He baptizes with water; Jesus baptizes with the Spirit (1:33). To miss this contrast is to miss the Johannine theology of ‘position’ enunciated through vivid contrasts.”¹³

“John’s joy is in fulfilling God’s will for his life—a model of Christian discipleship. He raises the question for all who would be disciples of Jesus, Where do we find our joy? It is easy to get distracted by the pleasurable blessings of this life. We should be thankful and receive gratefully God’s blessings, but our joy’s deepest foundation is God in himself. That he is as Jesus revealed him to be is our joy, as is the fulfilling of his purposes for our own lives (15:10-11), and we see this joy here in the Baptist.”¹⁴

“Notice that the word believes (v. 36) is not in contrast with does not believe but with rejects. An essential element of believing Jesus is accepting his word and obeying him. You can’t divorce obedience from belief. To believe you must obey what Jesus has commanded. What we believe and how we live are intertwined. Like strands woven together to make a rope, belief and obedience are woven together in salvation. The New Testament teaches that if you don’t turn from your sin to obey Jesus, then you haven’t put your faith in him.”¹⁵

The Old Testament portrays Yahweh as Israel’s faithful husband, though she was unfaithful. The prophet Hosea lived out this concept, when he obeyed God’s command to marry Gomer, an unfaithful woman (Hos. 1:2). The marriage represented God’s unwavering covenant relationship with Israel: Hosea, the faithful husband, represented God, and Gomer represented Israel, the adulterous wife. In today’s passage, John the Baptist compared himself to the groom’s friend and explained that he had no desire to distract the bride from the Groom (John 3:29). In ancient Hebrew culture, the groom’s friend often safely delivered the bride to the groom and stood watch outside their door on the night of the wedding. John’s job was to point the bride to the groom, Jesus. With a deep understanding of Scripture, John the Baptist built on the Old Testament theme; calling Jesus the Groom, the husband, acknowledged Him as God. Another interesting truth is that John the Baptist was both a friend of the Groom and also the bride, as are all believers!

The church is described as the bride of Christ, faithfully waiting for the day when Christ will return and heaven and earth will be one. Made up of all believers from all tongues and nations, the church is the bride that Christ redeemed. The picture of a bride also speaks to the permanence of Christ’s relationship with the church, for marriage was intended by God to be a lasting covenant between a man and a woman (Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:5).

God, we confess that sometimes we desire fame and glory. When we strive for the praise of others, convict us and remind us of our purpose. Help our lives point students to Jesus instead of pointing to ourselves. Remind us that anything good in us comes from you.

question.en: Let’s check in on how you’re doing spiritually. Last week, we talked about being an instrument of light as believers. Did you have opportunities to choose light (truth) over darkness (sin) last week? When did you struggle to make the right choice?

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You’ll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: If you could be famous for anything, what would it be and why?
Why do you think our culture is so interested in fame?
How does social media play a factor in making fame feel achievable?

content.en: Social media has contributed to many of us thinking fame is desirable and attainable. We’re sort of infatuated with the idea of influence. But fame and influence come with a price, often tempting us to seek glory for ourselves. Following Jesus means directing all glory to Him.

cultural_connection.en: Why do jealousy and competition exist between believers and in the church? Real answer: People are sinful; people make up the church. Jealousy creeps in, even between friends who follow Jesus. Maybe a friend is making an impact on others, and you feel jealous because you know his faults. Jealousy urges you to point them out instead of celebrating how God is changing your friend for the better and using him to help others. Maybe you desire attention and applause. You see people receiving attention for their good decisions, and you struggle with bitterness. Feeling jealous or competitive reveals our motive: We want the spotlight. Jealousy and competition harm the church, causing division and bitterness and shifting our focus off of Jesus and onto ourselves. We all struggle with these feelings, but we must recognize them immediately instead of allowing the feelings to simmer. We can confess how we feel to God and to the other person and ask God to help us shift our focus onto Him. We can clap for others and celebrate their wins. The truth is that following Jesus isn’t about attention or applause. Following Jesus means pointing to Him and away from ourselves because He is the One worthy of glory.

question.en: How does fame change people? What pressures come with it?

answer.en: We’ve watched people become famous overnight for a viral video or for a talent. Fame comes with the pressure of others watching everything you do and listening to everything you say. They see your wins, but they see your mistakes too. Sometimes, fame goes to our head, causing us to be arrogant. Fame can lead to the desire for more fame and more attention, even at the expense of our faith and our values. Worldly fame fades, too, just as quickly as we achieved it. Even if fame lasts for our lifetime, it means nothing in eternity. Striving for worldly fame distracts us from pointing to Jesus, the only One worthy of all fame.

question.en: How do John’s disciples seem to feel in verses 25-26?

answer.en: John explained that his purpose was to cry out in preparation for the Messiah (John 1:23). He didn’t desire glory and encouraged his followers to follow Jesus instead. But some of his disciples appeared bothered by the attention Jesus received, seeming to make it a contest. Maybe they felt betrayed by people who previously followed John. Maybe they felt jealousy over another rabbi rising in public opinion. Either way, they missed the point of John’s teaching. John was joyful that everyone was running to Jesus because that meant he was fulfilling his purpose. John showed us how to find joy by pointing to Jesus and away from ourselves.

question.en: How do churches and believers get caught in the trap of influencer culture, in seeking worldly fame or influence?

answer.en: Our culture is saturated with influencers. A quick scroll on social media exposes us to people being elevated because of their opinions about certain brands, songs, or political issues. We strive for influencer status. Churches and believers aren’t immune either. Influencer culture has helped create a celebrity Christianity. We measure impact by social media reactions and number of followers. If people don’t like and share our posts, then we aren’t influential. Sure, we can use social media as a platform to share the gospel, but how do we keep our motives pure? How do we not get caught in a desire for worldly fame—for attention, for more followers, for applause? The line gets blurry between pointing to the gospel and pointing to ourselves. The truth is that Jesus didn’t seek His own fame. He pointed to the Father. He lowered Himself, descended from a throne in heaven, and came here as a suffering Servant (Isa. 53). Consistent faithfulness in the small things isn’t small; serving when no one sees matters. Are we willing to decrease—to follow Jesus’s and John’s example? Or do we demand for the world to see our good works? If that’s our motive, then their applause is our only reward—applause we can’t carry with us when we go to heaven.

question.en: What does verse 31 show us about who we are in relation to who Jesus is? How should this impact the way we live?

answer.en: Verse 31 is clear that Jesus is above all—not just some things, some people, some of creation. Jesus has authority over all. He is God’s eternal Son, who reigns forever. Us? We’re earthly— created, temporary, finite, imperfect—yet, we often live like we are the ones in authority. We live as if we’re the center and everything revolves around us. The reality is that Jesus is the center, holding all things together (Col. 1:16-17). He speaks the words of the Father and shows us His character. Knowing this truth should cause us to reorient our lives to revolve around Jesus, to live according to the Word and not our opinions, to live with gladness under God’s good authority.

question.en: Read verse 36. How does the world teach very different ideas about getting to heaven or having eternal life?

answer.en: Verse 36 presents a choice: Believe in the Son or reject Him. Believing in Jesus as Lord leads to life, but rejecting Him as Lord leads to eternal wrath. Think of marriage: Marriage is the commitment of a man and a woman to one another. You’re either married to someone or not; there is no in- between, even if the world teaches otherwise. Scripture often compares believers to a bride and Jesus to the groom. We’re either in covenant relationship with Jesus or not. The world often teaches that many paths lead to “god,” who can exist in different forms. People believe they can go to heaven if they’re good people, but the truth is that none of us are good; we’ve all chosen sin (Rom. 3:23). Just as we’re either married or not married, we’re either the bride, committed to Jesus, or we’re not; vague middle ground isn’t an option.

question.en: How does our faithfulness to Jesus help Him “increase”? What does our unfaithfulness do?

answer.en: Jesus is above all; nothing we do changes His position. But our faithfulness to Jesus increases His name, or His reputation, in the world around us. We point to His glory and act as His ambassadors. When we’re unfaithful—when we live like the world—we harm God’s name and reputation because we spread a false idea of what it looks like to follow Him. We get to live in a way that increases Jesus’s name! Though God doesn’t need us, He chooses us as His ambassadors (2 Cor. 5:20)!

question.en: How can you use your influence to lift up Jesus instead of elevating yourself?

answer.en: This type of decrease is a choice. John chose to step out of the way and to direct all attention to Jesus. Why? Because Jesus is the One who matters— always. God may bless you with some amazing talents or skills. He may gift you with an ability to speak or to sing in front of large crowds. He may grant you opportunities that bring some type of fame. But what you do with attention and applause shows what’s at the center of your life: Jesus or yourself. If God gives you any sort of influence (and to some degree, He gives this to all of us), use it for His glory. Live faithfully, showing the world what a follower of Jesus looks like. Point others to Jesus, not just in your actions, but in your words; verbally share the gospel. God doesn’t desire for us to decrease in a harmful, demeaning, or self-deprecating way. God loves us and treasures us as His most unique creation, calling the day He created us “very good” (Gen. 1:31)! But may we never forget that our existence depends on Him. Our entire purpose is to give God glory—our influence for His name and not our own.

content.en:
Have you ever watched small children form a line? If so, you probably saw several of them race and push to be first in line. Being the line leader is a high privilege when we’re young! The position makes us feel powerful over our peers. Our world encourages us to elevate ourselves— to do whatever it takes to be first, to be seen, to be applauded. Jesus taught another way. In today’s passage, the mother of James and John, two of Jesus’s disciples, asked Jesus to promise that her sons would have seats next to His throne in the future kingdom. She wanted her sons to have the highest place of honor. Jesus used this moment to teach an important, radical truth: If we desire to be great, then we must serve and put others first. This concept was backwards and went against cultural norms. Jesus made the point that even He, the Son of God, came to serve and to give His life for others. He calls us to do the same—to lay down the desire for recognition in exchange for serving others, even when we receive no applause.

Think for just a moment about what happens when you receive attention from others. Sure, attention feels good and can encourage us to keep going, but more often, pride starts to sink in. We begin to make unwise decisions, hurting not only ourselves but others too. Now, think of a time when you served or helped others out of the desire for God to use you. Chances are not only did that feel better than becoming prideful but you likely felt greater peace and purpose. The Bible teaches us that Jesus should be elevated above all things. We can and should pursue great dreams and goals and strive for success. But we do these things to elevate Jesus and show Him to others. When we point to Jesus instead of to ourselves, we enjoy lasting satisfaction rather than fleeting applause from others.

question.en: Think of a time when you elevated yourself over others. How did that make you feel?
What does it say about our motives if serving others matters only when others see it and applaud?

prayer.en: Lord, forgive me for putting myself first, even before you. Thank you for Jesus’s example of how to serve others. Help me to point to you instead of to myself!

content.en:
What separates humans from every other creature is that we are made in God’s image. It’s not that animals, bugs, birds, fish and other things don’t matter; they just aren’t made in God’s image! We’re the only ones who get to be God’s managers for everything on earth. Only humans love others the way that God does. How? Because of Jesus living in us. If this is true (and it is), then that means that every single human in the world matters!

In our culture, we are often tempted to elevate ourselves over others. We may think that we have more to offer or are better than other people because of the country, the town, or the neighborhood we live in. This is a very dangerous mindset because none of these things matter when it comes to our eternity. The car we drive, the shoes and clothes we wear, the perfect test scores, and the state championship can’t make us right with God. Only a relationship with Jesus can do this. Jesus repeatedly called out religious leaders for viewing themselves as better than others. We must examine if we’re guilty of the same.

Paul taught what this idea looks like. If we are walking with Jesus, then loving and serving others should come naturally. Why? Because walking with Jesus—really learning from Jesus— transforms us to live like He lived. Jesus modeled humility by coming to the world as a human, living a life of service and love to others, and then dying on a cross for our sins. If He is our example and He lives in us, then we should strive to live humbly too.

question.en: In what ways have you considered yourself better than others lately? Why is this a problem, especially for believers?
How can you imitate the ways Jesus served and loved others this week?

prayer.en: Lord, I’m humbled when I remember that I have a heart problem only you can fix. Please rid me of my pride so I can live a life of service to you and others.

content.en:
Have you ever been around people who brag constantly about the things they’re good at? Even when everyone recognizes their talents, they still feel the need to announce them. Maybe you’ve struggled with this too. The truth is that we all fight this part of our human nature. We are designed to recognize glory—God’s glory—but our common struggle is desiring glory for ourselves. You may be an all-star athlete or a straight-A student. Maybe you’re a great reader or the best baker in the world! The truth is that we’re all good at something because God placed within each of us certain abilities and gifts. How do we use these gifts and talents wisely and humbly instead of using them as billboards to announce our own goodness?

We can be confident in God’s gifts without being prideful. Pride celebrates our ability but godly confidence points to God’s ability. When we hoard applause for ourselves, we’re standing on our own ability, and the truth is that we will fail at some point. Our ability is limited. But when we humbly use the gifts God has given us, we let go of needing people’s approval. Instead, we stand on the firm foundation of God’s ability that will never fail us and on His approval. We are confident only because we’re not standing on our own goodness! When we do something really great, the glory should go to God’s name. Jesus lives in us, empowering and strengthening us for good works. Other people may notice our success, but we will have greater impact on others when we direct their gaze to Jesus. Instead of announcing our wins, we can use any applause or attention to invest in eternity, in spreading Jesus’s name. This week, walk in confidence because of God’s good work and His ability!

question.en: In your own words, what is the difference between being confident and being prideful?
What are you are really good at? How can you use this to point others to Jesus more than yourself?

prayer.en: Lord, thank you for giving me certain gifts and talents. I recognize that they come from you. Help me to use these gifts to point others to you.

content.en:
Ambition is the desire and determination to reach a goal. Is having ambition wrong? Well, no—and maybe. James, the brother of Jesus, explained that bitter envy, which is the jealous desire for what others have, and selfish ambition lead to all kinds of evil. The key word is selfish. So, we can determine that ambition and selfish ambition are rooted in different motives: One strives to lift up God and the other strives to lift up self. We’ve established that pride is rooted in sin and that we need to rid our hearts of it each day. Sin directs us to look only at ourselves—at our wants and our needs. In other words, sin reinforces selfishness. We wrestle with selfishness on a daily basis—in the big and small choices we make in our classes, at the lunch table, with our teammates, in our friendships, in our homes, with our siblings.

James wrote about the dangerous outcome of a selfish lifestyle. He explained that ambition rooted in selfishness leads to “disorder and every vile practice.” As crazy as that sounds, selfish ambition lures us into doing whatever it takes, even when it’s sinful, to look out for our own good. Selfish ambition leads us to comparing and competing against others. When we stop comparing our lives and successes to others, we fight feelings of bitter jealousy and selfish ambition. Why? Because we find fulfillment and peace in pleasing God, not in pleasing ourselves. This is the way forward: We center all of our ambition on lifting up Jesus’s name.

question.en: In what ways do you struggle with selfishness? How have you seen that bring you and others down?
What ambitions do you have in life? How can you center those goals on Jesus instead of on yourself?

prayer.en: Lord, reveal to me the greatest areas of selfishness in my life. Show me how selfishness brings me and others down. Give me grace to move forward and live a different way.

content.en:
We’ve been studying how glorifying the Lord fulfills us more than glorifying ourselves. In case you need a refresher, to glorify means to elevate above other things. You may wonder how glorifying someone else could possibly feel better than glorifying yourself, but we were created for this! God designed us to glorify Him, so we are most satisfied when we do what God designed us to do. God made us to enjoy Him forever, but sin distorts our view and convinces us that chasing worldly comforts will give us peace. Worldly comforts will always disappoint us because we weren’t designed to be satisfied by them. Let’s think about technology for a minute. Technology can be a great tool, but being addicted to it brings us down and affects our personal well-being. We seek validation from social media, but instead, we’re often left feeling like we’re not enough and comparing ourselves to other people. We seek joy and escape in video games, but they all come to an end. Our feelings of depression and anxiety remain. The truth is that we won’t—we can’t—find satisfaction and peace in worldly pleasures.

The writer in Psalm 96 experienced God’s goodness, especially in comparison to what the world offers. The writer was overwhelmed by God’s glory and power in creation. The psalmist reminds us that everything except the Lord and His kingdom will fade away. If you’ve experienced God’s goodness and His glory, then the worldly comforts you used to depend on won’t satisfy you anymore. They’ll come up short. Instead, you can look to God’s glory and join with creation in worshiping Him and proclaiming His goodness!

question.en: How have you experienced more satisfaction in God than in worldly comforts? Think of a specific time and reflect on that experience.
How can you daily remind yourself that God is better than everything else?

prayer.en: Lord, I’ve tasted and seen just how good you are, but I’m still prone to forget. Bring me back to what I know is true and help me to be a light in the darkness.
